explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul sends for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he says goodbye and leaves for Macedonia (Acts 20:1). He doesn't just slip out the back door after all that uproar. I think a little encouragement is a fine thing to leave behind.

I get it, baker. After an uproar in the city (Acts 19:29), you might expect some finger-wagging. But the text says Paul sent for the disciples and, after encouraging them, said goodbye (Acts 20:1). No scolding in sight, just encouragement.

Good guess, baker, since people get baptized in Acts, like the Ethiopian official in Acts 8:38. But this verse says Paul sent for the disciples and, after encouraging them, said goodbye (Acts 20:1). It's a farewell, and the word is encouraging. Paul keeps the water out of this one.

explanations.answer: The Jews form a plot against him
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Paul is about to sail for Syria when the Jews form a plot against him, so he decides to go back through Macedonia (Acts 20:3). Plans change, and Paul changes with them. I've had a batch plan fall apart, but never over a plot like that.

explanations.answer: A storm keeps the ships in port
explanations.explanation: Storms do show up in Acts, like the one at sea in Acts 27:14, but not here, baker. The text says the Jews formed a plot against him as he was about to sail for Syria, and that's why he went back through Macedonia (Acts 20:3). The weather isn't mentioned at all. The trouble came from people.

explanations.answer: The Spirit tells him to wait
explanations.explanation: Nice thinking, baker, but this verse doesn't say that. It says the Jews formed a plot against him as he was about to sail, so he decided to go back through Macedonia (Acts 20:3). The Spirit isn't mentioned in this moment. The plot is the reason the passage gives.

That's it, baker. The writer says, "…after the Feast of Unleavened Bread, we sailed from Philippi…" (Acts 20:6). Notice the "we" again, so the writer is on the boat too. I like a feast with a clear start and finish. It makes planning easier.

Close, baker, since the Bible names other feasts, like Tabernacles in Leviticus 23:34. But this verse names the Feast of Unleavened Bread as the one they sail after (Acts 20:6). Tabernacles doesn't come up here. Feasts are a lot to keep straight. I once mixed up two recipe cards and we don't talk about that batch.

Good try, baker, but that feast isn't in this verse. The text says they sailed from Philippi after the Feast of Unleavened Bread (Acts 20:6). That's the one to hold onto here. The Trumpets can stay quiet this time.

explanations.answer: He's ready to leave the next day
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The text says that since Paul was ready to leave the next day, he talked to them and kept on speaking until midnight (Acts 20:7). I think he had a lot to fit in before the road called him away. Midnight, friend. I've never kept an oven on that long without somebody yelling about the bill.

explanations.answer: The crowd keeps asking him questions
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a good lively night, baker. But the text says Paul talked to them and kept on speaking because he was ready to leave the next day (Acts 20:7). No questions are mentioned. It reads like Paul doing the talking.

explanations.answer: He's waiting for the others to arrive
explanations.explanation: Fair guess, baker, but that isn't the reason the text gives. It says that since Paul was ready to leave the next day, he talked to them and kept on speaking until midnight (Acts 20:7). His planned departure is the reason. Waiting on others isn't mentioned.

True, baker. The text says Eutychus, seated in the window, was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on (Acts 20:9). I think a window seat is a risky spot to get sleepy. Hold onto that detail, because it matters in a moment.

It's true, baker. The text says Eutychus was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on (Acts 20:9). He was seated in the window when it happened. No tricks in this one, just a very sleepy young man in a very risky spot.

I wish that were the case, baker, but it's false. The text says that when Eutychus fell from the third story, he "…was picked up dead." (Acts 20:9). This is a heavy part of the story. Hold on, though, because Paul is about to step in.

That's right, baker. The text says Eutychus fell from the third story and "…was picked up dead." (Acts 20:9). He wasn't just shaken up. I think this part of the story hurts, so it's worth slowing down here. The story isn't over, though.

explanations.answer: The young man is still alive
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says, "Do not be alarmed!" and then, "He is still alive!" (Acts 20:10). He goes down, throws himself on the young man and embraces him. Then he speaks, and what he says is good news for everybody in that room.

That's a kind thing to say, baker, but it's not what Paul says. He says, "Do not be alarmed!" and then, "He is still alive!" (Acts 20:10). Nobody is assigned any blame or cleared of it in the text. Paul goes straight to the news that matters.

I can see why you'd think so, baker, since comfort fits a moment like this. But Paul doesn't say that. After "Do not be alarmed!" he says, "He is still alive!" (Acts 20:10). The comfort comes with the news itself.

That's right, baker. After going back upstairs, breaking bread and eating, Paul speaks until daybreak, and then he departs (Acts 20:11). Midnight wasn't the end of it. A full night of talking after all that, and I can't even get through a double batch without a nap.

That would be a sensible choice, baker, but the text doesn't say it. Paul goes back upstairs, breaks bread, eats, and after speaking until daybreak, he departs (Acts 20:11). Speaking until daybreak is what comes next. The night keeps going.
Not quite, baker. Paul does leave, but not right away. First he goes back upstairs, breaks bread, eats and speaks until daybreak, and then he departs (Acts 20:11). Quite a night comes first.

That's the word, baker. The text says the people were greatly relieved to take the boy home alive (Acts 20:12). After what happened, I bet that relief was enormous. Alive is a very good word to hear after a night like that.

Puzzled would make sense if you're thinking about how strange the night was, baker. But the text says the people were greatly relieved to take the boy home alive (Acts 20:12). Relief is the word the passage gives. Being taken home alive is the whole point.

I see why that came to mind, baker, since earlier in the night the young man was picked up dead (Acts 20:9). But the text says the people were greatly relieved to take the boy home alive (Acts 20:12). Relief is the word the passage gives. Alive changes everything.
